author: Platform Documentation
deck: The platform can turn any article into a real, downloadable PDF -- free, instant, and with no AI model involved. It now supports multiple pages, photos, and tables, not just plain text on a single page.
description: How PDF generation works on this platform: a deterministic, zero-cost template render that now supports multiple pages, embedded images, and real tables, confirmed live with this article's own downloadable PDF.

image.alt: Photo illustration of layered documents and printed pages, representing an article turned into a polished, multi-page PDF.

public.body: Everything on this platform lives as a web page by default. But sometimes what you actually want is a document — something a reader can download, save, print, or forward without opening a browser. The platform can produce that: a real PDF, generated from the same written content, through the same governed object system as everything else.
public.title: Content doesn't have to stay on the page

public.body: A PDF here is built from a template — a layout with named fields — plus the data that fills those fields in. Nothing about turning text into a laid-out page requires a model to run: it's a direct, mechanical render, the same "already known, so a rule can do it" principle covered in the platform's article on what needs AI and what doesn't. That means generating a PDF costs nothing and returns in seconds, the same whether it's generated once or a hundred times.
public.title: How it actually works

public.body: A generated PDF is no longer limited to a single page of plain text. It can flow across as many pages as an article actually needs, and each page can include more than paragraphs: photos, colored panels, dividing lines, and real tables, all in the site's own colors. A short field guide can still fit on one page if that is all it needs. A longer guide, like this one, can spread out, include a picture, and close with a clean comparison table, all generated automatically from the article itself.
public.title: What it can do now

public.body: The two gaps described in earlier drafts of this article are fixed and confirmed live. The renderer now recognizes every element type it is supposed to (text, images, colored boxes, dividing lines, and tables), and the bug that used to quietly drop every page after the first has been corrected. The proof is this very document: it was generated fresh, as a three-page PDF with a photo on the cover and a real comparison table on the closing page. Download it from the button below and you get a live example, not a mockup.
public.title: What Changed, Now Confirmed Live

public.body: Rendered from this site's own on-brand pdfme template, using the platform's real colors, through the same artifact-job pipeline described above. This is the multi-page version: three pages, a sharper cover photo, and a comparison table, generated the same way any editor can generate one from their own article.
public.title: Download This Article as a PDF

public.body: Nothing about how you'd ask for a PDF needs to change when multi-page layouts and embedded graphics become available — the request stays the same; only what comes back gets richer. Until then, a single well-designed page, in the site's own colors, is the honest ceiling, and it's still a real, working, free document — not a placeholder.
public.title: What changes once the gaps close
